entries.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of a Rectangular Pulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the continuous-time Fourier transform of a finite rectangular pulse by evaluating the transform integral over the pulse interval and converting the result into a scaled sinc spectrum with the correct amplitude, width, and phase.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Zeros of the Rectangular Pulse Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Teach that the rectangular pulse spectrum's zeros come from the sine numerator and solve for the nonzero angular-frequency roots.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the zero locations follow directly from the sinc-form spectrum.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how to read the zero condition from the rectangular pulse spectrum, then solve $\sin(\omega T/2)=0$ for the nonzero roots.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the width-$T$ rectangular pulse spectrum already written in sinc form and focus on the simplest nonzero root pair before generalizing.
paragraph_plan: Recall the sinc-form spectrum from the previous lesson and point to the factor that can vanish.
State that zeros occur when the sine numerator is zero, not when the whole fraction is naively treated as zero at $\omega=0$.
Solve $\omega T/2=k\pi$ to obtain the indexed zero family $\omega_k=2\pi k/T$.
Exclude $k=0$ and note that the first nonzero zeros are the symmetric pair at $k=\pm 1$.
Preview that the same formula also gives the constant null spacing $\Delta\omega=2\pi/T$ used in the next examples.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation symbolic and compact, reuse the sinc-zero fact from the prior lesson, and emphasize that $k=0$ is not a zero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: angular-frequency values

Drop the sign symmetry and give only the positive root.
Include $\omega=0$ even though it is not a zero.
Substitute the width incorrectly after solving the root condition.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A rectangular pulse has width $T=6$. Find the first nonzero angular-frequency zeros of its spectrum.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the first nonzero zeros are $\omega=\pm 2\pi/T$, so for $T=6$ they are $\omega=\pm\pi/3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the abstract zero condition in the tutorial to a concrete width and asks only for the first nonzero pair.
solution_step_plan: Start from $\sin(\omega T/2)=0$.
Solve $\omega T/2=k\pi$ and isolate $\omega=2\pi k/T$.
Choose $k=\pm1$ for the first nonzero pair.
Substitute $T=6$ and simplify to $\omega=\pm\pi/3$.
practice_variation_axes: Different pulse widths with the same zero-condition algebra.
Ask for the first nonzero pair versus the full zero set.
Mix exact symbolic widths with clean numerical widths.

sections.section_title: Finding the Full Zero Pattern of a Rectangular Pulse Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Write the full indexed family of nonzero zeros for a rectangular pulse spectrum.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the full zero pattern is an indexed symbolic family.

question_policy.answer_format: indexed formula
question_policy.practice_question_model: A rectangular pulse of width $T=4$ has spectrum $X(j\omega)=A T\frac{\sin(\omega T/2)}{\omega T/2}$. Which expression gives the full set of nonzero angular-frequency zeros?
distractor_plan: Use the correct family but include $k=0$.
Miss the factor of 2 and write $\omega_k=\pi k/T$.
Confuse the zero set with the spacing and give only a spacing statement.
List only the first pair instead of the full indexed family.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A rectangular pulse has width $T=6$. Write the full set of nonzero angular-frequency zeros of its spectrum.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that every nonzero zero is $\omega_k=2\pi k/T$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$, which for $T=6$ gives $\omega_k=k\pi/3$ for nonzero integers $k$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the first-pair result to the entire zero family and makes the integer indexing explicit.
solution_step_plan: Start from the general root condition $\omega_k=2\pi k/T$.
State that $k$ can be any nonzero integer.
Substitute $T=6$ to get $\omega_k=k\pi/3$.
List the first few positive and negative zeros to make the pattern visible.
practice_variation_axes: Different widths that change the index spacing.
Ask for the general formula instead of the first pair.
Ask the learner to identify the full nonzero set from a partially listed pattern.

sections.section_title: Computing Null Spacing from Pulse Width
sections.learning_goal: Compute the constant angular-frequency gap between adjacent spectral zeros.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the spacing comes directly from subtracting consecutive zeros.

question_policy.answer_format: angular-frequency spacing value
question_policy.practice_question_model: A rectangular pulse of width $T=9$ has spectral zeros at constant spacing. What is the angular-frequency spacing between adjacent zeros?
distractor_plan: Use the reciprocal $T/(2\pi)$ instead of $2\pi/T$.
Drop the factor of 2 and use $\pi/T$.
Confuse spacing with the first zero location.
Leave the answer unsimplified and numerically inconsistent.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A rectangular pulse has width $T=6$. What is the spacing between adjacent nonzero zeros of its spectrum?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that consecutive zeros differ by $\Delta\omega=2\pi/T$, so for $T=6$ the spacing is $\pi/3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Switches from locating individual zeros to measuring the gap between neighboring zeros.
solution_step_plan: Write two consecutive zeros as $\omega_k=2\pi k/T$ and $\omega_{k+1}=2\pi(k+1)/T$.
Subtract to get $\Delta\omega=\omega_{k+1}-\omega_k$.
Simplify the difference to $\Delta\omega=2\pi/T$.
Substitute $T=6$ and simplify to $\pi/3$.
practice_variation_axes: Different widths that change the spacing value.
Ask for spacing from the formula or from two listed zeros.
Mix symbolic and numerical pulse widths.

sections.handoff_notes: Use adjacent-zero subtraction to expose the constant spacing directly.

sections.section_title: Inferring Pulse Width from Null Spacing
sections.learning_goal: Recover the pulse width from the spacing between adjacent spectral zeros.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the pulse width is recovered algebraically from the spacing relation.

question_policy.answer_format: pulse width value

Drop the factor of 2 and give $T=\pi/\Delta\omega$.
Confuse the spacing value with the width itself.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: The spacing between adjacent nonzero zeros of a rectangular pulse spectrum is $\Delta\omega=\pi/3$. Find the pulse width $T$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Invert $\Delta\omega=2\pi/T$ to obtain $T=2\pi/\Delta\omega$, then compute $T=6$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverses the spacing relation so the learner solves for the width instead of the gap.
solution_step_plan: Start from $\Delta\omega=2\pi/T$.
Solve algebraically for $T$.
Substitute $\Delta\omega=\pi/3$.
Check that the result is $T=6$ and that the units are consistent.
practice_variation_axes: Different spacings that still invert cleanly.
Ask for width from spacing rather than spacing from width.
Include spacing values that tempt a factor-of-two error.

sections.handoff_notes: Reverse the spacing formula cleanly and verify the reciprocal relationship before finishing.
